about.title: Corona Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Corona sits where SR-91 meets I-15, and the shopping centers, warehouses, and apartment communities that have grown up around those interchanges see a lot of foot traffic. But a wet entryway at a Main Street market, a broken stair at a rental complex, or an unlit pothole in a parking lot can change an ordinary errand in seconds. Under California premises liability law, the property owner is not automatically at fault when someone falls. You generally have to show the owner knew about the hazard, or reasonably should have known, and failed to repair it or post a warning. That is why what you do in the first days matters so much. Photograph the spot, note the time, ask for an incident report, and request that any surveillance footage be preserved before it is recorded over. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects Corona residents with an independent attorney who handles premises cases on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Corona Residents Use LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Notice Is the Heart of the Case
items.desc: California requires proof that the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. The attorneys we connect you with know how to look for inspection logs, prior complaints, and maintenance records that show what the property owner was aware of.

items.title: Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many Corona businesses and apartment complexes record over surveillance footage within days or weeks. Getting an attorney involved early means a preservation request can go out before that evidence is gone.

items.title: Deadlines and Shared Fault Are Manageable
items.desc: You generally have two years to file, and far less if a public entity is involved. California's pure comparative fault rule also means you may still recover even if you were partly distracted or hurried when you fell.

items.question: I fell on a cracked sidewalk maintained by the City of Corona. Is the deadline different?
items.answer: Yes, and it is much shorter. When a public entity such as the city or Riverside County controls the property, California requires a formal government claim first, usually within six months of the injury. Missing that window can end the case before it begins, so it is worth speaking with an attorney quickly rather than waiting to see how your injuries heal.

items.question: The store says I should have been watching where I was walking. Does that end my claim?
items.answer: Not by itself. California follows pure comparative fault, so a jury or insurer can assign you a percentage of responsibility and reduce your recovery by that share rather than eliminate it. If a spill sat unmarked in a Main Street grocery aisle for an hour, the owner's failure to clean it or post a cone still counts, even if you were looking at your phone.

items.question: I did not take pictures at the scene. Can anything still be done?
items.answer: Often, yes. Go back and photograph the location as soon as you safely can, since conditions like broken tiles or missing handrails tend to stay put. An attorney can also send a letter demanding that the property owner preserve surveillance video, incident reports, and cleaning schedules, and can track down witnesses who saw the hazard before you did.
